## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the best swell direction.
- Sources disagree about the best wind direction.
- Sources disagree about the wave size this break works in.
- Limited information is available about the swell period this break needs.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> All 7 readable current sources were re-read and 2 new ones added: Yeeew and Hawaii Life. WIND: readable sources agree on a southerly offshore: Surf-Forecast SSW, WSL BWT guide calm winds from the south, WannaSurf S and Yeeew S. The only contradiction is Surfertoday's E-SE (403, unchanged). Several WSL pages note that strong trades are the usual problem. SWELL DIRECTION CONFLICT: WSL (Surfline text) says the window opens about 305 and 320+ is best, so the profile window min of 290 may be too wide. WannaSurf, Yeeew and Hawaii Life say N, within 15 deg of the 315-345 optimum. Surf-Forecast's NNE (22.5) is outside the optimum and recorded as contradicting. WSL says westerly sets barrel. SIZE: 60+ ft faces (Wikipedia, WSL x2). Yeeew says good from triple overhead (about 18 ft faces, converted). WannaSurf says over 12 ft, scale unstated, not compared. WSL says the reef handles any size. PERIOD: still only qualitative (groundswell). No readable source gives seconds; buoy readings in event stories (Flux Hawaii) were not recorded. TIDE: 'all' from Surf-Forecast, WannaSurf and Yeeew. BATHYMETRY: WSL trench 100->20 ft, WSL underwater ridge NW of Maui, Wikipedia underwater ridge studied by scientists. The Fearing & Dalrymple Univ. of Delaware refraction study could not be reached and the USGS WRI 2000-4046 Maui bathymetry has no abstract. Not readable (403): Surfertoday, ResearchGate, mondo.surf.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 12 ft [S7] · 30 ft [S3] · triple overhead [S9] | conflicting | S3, S7, S9 | `wave_height_min_ft` 20 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | triple overhead and bigger, with no upper limit | documented | S9 | no separate setting; working range 20–60 ft |
| Maximum suitable | no upper limit: the reef handles any swell; faces reach 60 ft or more (up to 80 ft per Surfertoday) (face where stated) | documented | S1, S3, S4, S5, S6 | `wave_height_max_ft` 60 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at over 3.5 m / 12 ft (scale not stated), Surfertoday (search summary) says the waves range from 30 to 80 ft, and Yeeew says it gets good from triple overhead (relative face height, no number).
  - S7 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at Over 3.5m / 12ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over”
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “Waves range between 30 and 80 feet”
  - S9 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between triple overhead and however big the swell is.”
- **Ideal range**: Yeeew says it gets good between triple overhead and however big the swell is; no number in feet is given.
  - S9 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between triple overhead and however big the swell is.”
- **Maximum suitable**: WSL says the reef can handle as big a swell as the ocean can throw at it and that the waves reach upwards of 60 ft on the face (60 ft or more), Wikipedia that they can exceed 60 ft, and Surfertoday (search summary) that they range up to 80 ft; no source states a size at which the break stops working.
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The wave sizes at Jaws (which can exceed 60 feet (18 m) during the months of December to March)”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “molds large winter swells into spinning, blue behemoths that reach upwards of 60 feet on the face”
  - S6 (World Surf League): “The wave can reach heights of 60 feet or more.”
  - S4 (World Surf League): “The reef can handle as big a a swell as the ocean can throw at it, but often the wind gets too strong to paddle”
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “Waves range between 30 and 80 feet”

### Swell direction

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideal bearing | 0–22.5° (N to NNE, clockwise) | documented | S2, S7, S9, S10 | `optimal_swell_direction` 315–345° (NW to NNW, clockwise) |
| Acceptable range | 270–45° (W to NE, clockwise) | documented | S3, S5 | `swell_window` 290–30° (WNW to NNE, clockwise) |
| Blocked directions | — | not documented | — | no separate setting (outside `swell_window`) |
| Exposure | deep-water reef jutting straight into the North Pacific | documented | S5 | no setting |

Notes:

- **Ideal bearing**: WannaSurf (good) and Yeeew (best) say north and Hawaii Life says large north swells make the big waves, while Surf-Forecast gives north-northeast (22.5 deg) as best; the value spans N to NNE.
  - S7 (WannaSurf): “Good swell directionNorth”
  - S9 (Yeeew!): “The best swells are from the North.”
  - S10 (Hawaii Life Vacations): “Large north swells which produce big waves at Jaws typically occur during the winter months.”
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “the best swell direction is from the north northeast”
- **Acceptable range**: Surfertoday (search summary) says it works best with northern (NW-NE) swells and that the lefts need a swell arriving from the west, and WSL says the wave barrels when a set swings west; the value spans W (270 deg) clockwise to NE (45 deg).
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “Jaws is predominantly a right-hand barreling wave and works best with northern (NW-NE) swells and southeasterly (E-SE) winds.”
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “Left-handers need a different angle: the swell should be arriving from the west.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Jaws is one of the few big-wave spots with a proper barrel, and when a set swings west, the local surfers have every intention of pulling in.”
- **Blocked directions**: No excerpt names swell directions that are blocked or shadowed by land or reefs.
- **Exposure**: WSL says Pe'ahi's deep-water, triangular reef juts straight into the North Pacific.
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Pe'ahi's deep-water, triangular reef juts straight into the North Pacific”

### Geography

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Break type | reef (rights and lefts, predominantly right) | documented | S2, S3, S7, S10 | `break_type` reef, `wave_direction` both |
| Orientation | — | not documented | — | nearshore-model shore normal estimated as the centre of the optimal swell direction (330° (NNW)) |
| Exposure | triangular deep-water reef jutting straight into the North Pacific | documented | S5 | no setting |
| Bathymetry | deep trench close to shore rising from about 100 ft to 20 ft; an underwater ridge reaching NW of Maui refracts the swell; coral reef | documented | S1, S4, S5, S6, S8, S9, S10 | no measured bathymetry (profile derived from the swell windows) |

Notes:

- **Break type**: Surf-Forecast and Hawaii Life say the reef gives rights and lefts, WannaSurf lists a fast, powerful right, and Surfertoday (search summary) calls it predominantly a right-hand barrel.
  - S2 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Reef breaks provide lefts and rights.”
  - S10 (Hawaii Life Vacations): “The seafloor topography at Jaws is unique in that it amplifies the incoming swell energy to create well-formed waves which break to the right as well as to the left.”
  - S7 (WannaSurf): “DirectionRight...PowerFast, Powerful...Normal lengthVery Long (300 to 500 m)”
  - S3 (Surfertoday): “Jaws is predominantly a right-hand barreling wave and works best with northern (NW-NE) swells and southeasterly (E-SE) winds.”
- **Orientation**: No excerpt states which way the coast or the break faces.
- **Exposure**: WSL says the reef juts straight into the North Pacific.
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Pe'ahi's deep-water, triangular reef juts straight into the North Pacific”
- **Bathymetry**: WSL describes a deep trench rising from about 100 ft to 20 ft and an underwater ridge to the northwest that refracts the swell, Wikipedia says the ridge has been studied, the Caldwell & Aucan paper (search summary) cites Fearing (2000)'s refraction/diffraction model, Yeeew says the waves break over coral reef and Hawaii Life that the seafloor amplifies the swell; no depth survey is quoted.
  - S4 (World Surf League): “There is an extremely deep trench uncommonly close to shore, which comes up from around 100 feet to 20 feet.”
  - S6 (World Surf League): “Its enormity comes from a large underwater ridge that reaches out to the northwest of Maui and causes the deep water of the Pacific to refract and bend”
  - S1 (Wikipedia): “The extreme size of the waves is caused by the structure of an underwater ridge which has been studied by scientists.”
  - S8 (ResearchGate (Journal of Coastal Research paper, Caldwell & Aucan)): “wave refraction at Jaws, Maui, Hawaii has been quantified by Fearing, (2000) using a combined refraction/diffraction model”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Pe'ahi's deep-water, triangular reef juts straight into the North Pacific”
  - S9 (Yeeew!): “The waves here break for up to 200 meters over a coral reef.”
  - S10 (Hawaii Life Vacations): “The seafloor topography at Jaws is unique in that it amplifies the incoming swell energy to create well-formed waves which break to the right as well as to the left.”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell height · minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at over 3.5 m / 12 ft (scale not stated), Surfertoday (search summary) says the waves range from 30 to 80 ft, and Yeeew says it gets good from triple overhead (relative face height, no number).
- **Wind · offshore**: WSL (calm winds from the south), WannaSurf (good: south), Yeeew (best: south) and Surf-Forecast (offshore SSW) agree on a southerly, while Surfertoday (search summary) says it works best with southeasterly (E-SE) winds.

## Judgement check

Every field's excerpts were re-read on 2026-10-27. Changes:

- swell_direction.acceptable_range: 315-45 deg -> 270-45 deg; two of the three cited excerpts say west swells work (lefts, west-swinging sets), so W belongs in the working range.
- swell_height.max_suitable: 60-80 ft -> 'no upper limit' with the reported 60-80 ft faces; the excerpts describe the largest waves, not a maximum suitable size.
